lectures.title: A Brief Look at the Remix Config File

cues.en: Now before we'll dive
into a concrete deployment example,
there's one last thing we should take a look at
and that's the Remix config file,
the configuration we can apply to Remix.
Now arguably the best place to dive deeper
on that is the official documentation
because most of these conflict settings
are only needed in niche scenarios.
So that's the best place to learn about all of them.
But there are three settings here
which I do wanna highlight.
The first setting is this ignore route files setting
which is actually enabled by default
and which by default ignores all files
in the route folder that start with a dot.
What this setting does is, it simply defines which files
in the route folder will not be treated as routes,
because by default all files in there
will be treated as routes.
But this setting, for example,
ensures that files starting with a dot will be ignored.
So invisible files, you could say.
We could also add a pattern like this
to ignore any CSS files in that folder
so that if we planned to have a specific CSS files
next to our component files
we could do that without adding any new routes here.
If we add the appropriate setting here in Remix config JS
we will ignore those CSS files just fine.
And you can add as many settings here
as many to be ignored files as you want.
So that's the first setting that's worth a closer look.
Another interesting setting
is the assets built directory setting,
which is by default not enabled
but there is a default setting for this setting.
It's just not overwritten.
Now here you could override the default path
for the build output of Remix
and we will run a build command
in the next lecture again,
to prepare the application for deployment.
And what that build command will do is
it will generate a couple of optimized JavaScript files
that in the end also make up our application.
Now, if you plan to deploy your application
such that your public files, like for example, images,
that should be accessible to everyone
are not stored in a folder named public,
then you should also update this path
to ensure that this build path
is in the folder that will be publicly accessible.
Because the output, the build output here
must be in such a publicly accessible folder.
So therefore, by default you don't need to change this
but if you plan on using some other folder than public
you would need to update this build output path
setting here as well.
And the last setting which I wanna highlight
is this server dependencies to bundle setting.
It's not commented out here in this default setting
which I have here, but we could nonetheless
add it here, this server dependencies to bundle setting.
And what this setting does is
it allows you to specify an array of identifiers
that identify third party packages
you might have in your package dot JSON file
which do not support common JS.
Now, common JS is basically an approach
for importing JavaScript files into each other
and an approach for combining JavaScript files.
The alternative is ES modules.
Now the import export syntax we used in this course
with the import statement is actually ES modules
though not really, we're just using this here
during development, but behind the scenes it is translated
to a different syntax, to the common JS syntax.
You don't need to know the details
but it is important to understand that
there are these two different systems for combining files.
And under the hood, at least at the point of time
I'm recording this, Remix uses common JS.
There are some third party packages
which don't support this system though
and which therefore could cause errors.
We don't have them here in this project
but such packages exist.
And if you do get such errors where you basically
get complaints about a package being ESM only,
then you can simply add that package name here
to server dependencies to bundle,
so that Remix will treat it differently
behind the scenes you could say.
So it's also setting you probably don't need all the time
but for certain packages you might need it.
And since I don't want you to encounter this
ESM package error without knowing what you can do,
I wanted to show this setting as well.
But that's it for this configuration.
Now let's take a look at an example deployment.
When it comes to deploying Remix apps,
you have different choices.
To be precise, when you create a Remix application with npx
create Remix at latest,
you don't just get asked for the name of your project
but you also get asked where you want to deploy it.
Now the list of options here might change over time,
but in general, Remix supports different deployment targets.
Now, you can use the Remix app server and deploy your app
on any hosting machine that supports node JS.
But you can also choose more specific deployment provider,
which often makes deployment a bit easier than
if you run your own node JS server, for example, Netlify.
And if you wanna deploy
to such a target to Netlify for example,
you should create a project where you make that choice.
And that's exactly what I'm doing here.
I'm creating a new project where I chose Netlify
as the deployment target
and then add your code to that project.
If you already have a Remix project where
you chose a different deployment target, as it's the case
for us here, you can simply copy over your app folder,
your public folder, in our case, the prisma folder
and also our dependencies, and you're good to go.
So you can copy that over
and then use that provider in that project.
And we'll do that in just a second.
Now, Remix supports deployment
to different platforms through a feature called adapters.
And as mentioned, we'll probably see more possible targets
over time, and you can also build your own adapter
which of course is a bit more advanced, but you can look
into this adapter or configuration to learn more about that.
Here we're now going to deploy this application to Netlify
so that we see one example deployment process in action.

lectures.title: Deploying a Remix Website - An Example (Netlify)

cues.en: Now to deploy to Netlify here,
I'll start by copying my app folder,
and my public folder and my prisma folder.
And if I had made any changes to remix.config.js
that file as well,
to that other project which I created for Netlify.
So I'll copy that over
and make sure to replace any existing files.
And then I'll open this remix deployment project.
And then there in the package.json file
I want to add my extra dependencies.
Now, I did not just replace this package.json file
because there are some Netlify specific dependencies
in there which I did not want to lose.
But I'll add any extra dependencies which I have here
by simply pasting them in here like this.
And I can then simply remove any duplicates
I might have here.
There should be no difference for the dev dependencies.
And with that,
we prepared this project for deployment to Netlify.
Now in order to deploy it now, we then have to go
to the Netlify website and create an account there.
Now you could log in with GitHub
up or create a new account with email and password
and I'll actually choose GitHub here.
But for that, I'll first of all create a new
GitHub account where I wanna host my
Netlify project anyways.
So this project which I wanna deploy
because we'll then link Netlify to GitHub
so that Netlify can pull the code from GitHub.
So therefore here I'll quickly create a GitHub account.
And of course you can also use an existing one.
And then here in my account
I'll simply create a new repository
in my case here, a private one
which I'll name remix Netlify example, like this.
And I'll then connect this
to my local project and push my code to GitHub.
Now, I'll not show all the details of how that works
since this is not a GitHub course, but in the end
you simply need to add this repository
as a remote repository to your project
and then push your code to GitHub.
With that done, I got my code on GitHub
which is an important prerequisite
to connecting it to Netlify and to ensuring that
Netlify gets access to this code.
And I can now log into Netlify here
with my GitHub account.
Authorize Netlify to access my account
and then import a project from GitHub.
And here after authorizing Netlify again,
I'll select this repository which I just added
which contains my code.
And I'll in the end link it to Netlify here.
Now, here I wanna deploy the main branch
so the code in the main branch
and it automatically detects that this is a remix project
and therefore understands how to build that project
and how to then serve all the files.
And therefore then we can click deploy site.
And now this project is being built and deployed by Netlify.
However, right now this is not all we have to do.
Instead, we also have to log into our MongoDB account again
because since our application will now soon be served
by Netlify servers we also must allow those servers
to connect to our databases.
And for that, under network access,
we also have to allow access from anywhere to our database
not just from our local IP.
Otherwise connection attempts from our application running
on the Netlify servers will fail.
And we of course don't want that.
So therefore, now with that being update, if I go back
to Netlify and reload, it looks like the app was deployed.
I also get a link here.
You can of course also add your own domain if you want to
but here I get an automatically generated domain
and I get an error regarding prisma not being initialized.
The reason for that is that prisma needs to run
this command to build this package
which we use in our code to interact with prisma.
To fix this, we should go back to our project
to this Netlify remix project, which we created.
And there in this Netlify.toml which you have in there
change this build command here, from remix build,
to npx prisma generate
and and remix build
so that this command will be executed
before we trigger the build.
Because this command will then generate the
prisma package that's needed by our code to work.
With that done, we can add and create a new commit.
But before we push this
we also have to change something back there on Netlify.
There you should go to site, settings, and then there
scroll down all the way to environment
and there click on added variables,
under environment variables.
And there are two environment variables which
we've been using in this project.
We must set them here for production as well.
We must add the database URL
and send it to the same URL as before.
Of course, we could also use a different user and password
if we had different users and passwords set up on MongoDB
but we must have a valid connection URL here.
And we also must specify the session secret.
Otherwise, our code will crash when we try to work
with sessions.
And here this should be set
to some secure value and that should be saved as well.
So that's another important thing we have to do
besides editing this build command.
So now that the environment variables were updated
we should push our updated code here.
And since Netlify is linked to our GitHub repository,
this will automatically trigger a new deployment process.
We can see this here under deploys
and this time this should succeed.
So now that this new deployment process finished
we can visit this website again, and this looks much better.
That's our website up and running.
We can navigate around.
We can also log in all with our existing users
because we're still using the same database.
So these users still exist, the expenses still exist.
Of course, we can delete them though.
We can add new expenses
and we can do all the things we did throughout this course.
But now in our deployed remix application here
at the example of Netlify.
Congratulations, you finished this course,
and you learned a lot about Remix day four.
You learned all the essentials
and also many advanced features,
and therefore you have all you need to start building
your own Remix applications and dive deeper into Remix.
And definitely keep on using Remix.
Keep on practicing Remix, build demo and dummy projects
because that is how you will learn the most.
Definitely also try rebuilding the course projects
without looking at the lectures,
because that can be a great practice as well,
because ultimately this course can only give
you the foundation.
You then need to practice what you learned,
so that you can really grow and learn more and more
about Remix and development in general.
That being said, I hope you liked the course.
I hope you got a lot out of it, and I would
of course love to welcome you back in other courses,
like my React or next JS courses, but either way,
I wish you all the best for your future.
